lines.text: Both wheels of a train are locked to one solid axle, so they always spin together. So how does it turn a corner?
On a curve, the outer rail is longer. Flat wheels would have to skid to keep up.
The trick: train wheels aren't flat. They're cones, wider on the inside.
In a curve, the wheels slide outward, so the outer wheel rolls on its wide part, the inner on its narrow part.
Wider means more distance per turn, so the outer side travels farther, and the train steers itself around the bend.
On straight track, the same cones keep nudging the wheels back to the middle.
But at high speed, that nudging can overshoot into a violent side to side wobble, called hunting.
